@geraldcombs https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/4080

So this supports random access to Zstandard or LZ4-compressed files, right?

If so, is it fast random access, or does seeking backward involve rewinding the file and moving sequentially forward to the new position?
...and should this be mentioned in docbook/release-notes.adoc?

Yes it's supports random access, but not fast rewinding, there is no API for that in ZSTD or LZ4. Performance is fine in the wireshark UI, remember that zstd and lz4 has single core decompression speeds in the 1-4GB/s range.
We should probably mention compression support here too https://www.wireshark.org/docs/wsug_html_chunked/ChIOOpenSection.html#ChIOInputFormatsSection

> Yes it's supports random access, but not fast rewinding

Rewinding and sequentially scanning forward *isn't* a fast way to do backward seeks.  Consider Wireshark having just read the last packet in the random-access stream and then reading the packet just before that packet.  That's fast with a gzip (zlib) file.

> Performance is fine in the wireshark UI

Have you tried compressing a multi-gigabyte file, opening it in Wireshark, selecting the last packet, and then manually going backward through the list, one packet at a time?  Is the performance for that fine?  If so, then you do support fast random access.

> remember that zstd and lz4 has single core decompression speeds in the 1-4GB/s range.

Decompression isn't the only overhead here; just reading data from the file costs both I/O (if the file is big enough that it doesn't fit in the buffer cache/page pool) and CPU (system call overhead, copying the data), and seeking backwards from the last packet to the previous packet - or, at least, a packet that's not in the current decompressed buffer - involves a lot of that for a large file.

Wireshark is not IO bound when loading compressed or uncompressed files. On Linux drop caches, launch iotop and open a multigigabyte pcap and you'll see.

I tested the UI with a 1.2GiB pcap that compresses down to 70M with zstd -9 (I typically see ~1:10 ratio for my use case) and I didn't notice any slowdown when I did your test. Maybe it won't work with 10GiB files, but I would say that's a rare use case. I always extract the subset I need using tshark/tcpdump/etc since wireshark UI is pretty sluggish beyond 200MiB large pcaps.

> I tested the UI with a 1.2GiB pcap that compresses down to 70M with zstd -9 (I typically see \~1:10 ratio for my use case) and I didn't notice any slowdown when I did your test.

I tested it with a 740 MiB file that compresses down to 194 MiB with zstd -9, and if I go to the end of the file, select the last packet, and click the up-arrow button, there's a close-to-1-second delay for each click.

If I test it with the same file compressed with gzip down to 253 MiB, and do the same test, there's no noticeable delay when clicking the up-arrow button.

Yeah I'm sure there will be differences depending on the CPU. There are ways to improve this in the future. Wireshark already stores the dissection result in RAM, it can also cache the packet data for compressed files. The cache could be all packets recompressed to say 1MiB chunks using LZ4 or LRU with "fault around" like the Linux page cache. IO should also be done off the main thread, so the UI is always responsive.

@AndersBroman @geraldcombs @guyharris Thank you everyone for reviewing this and merging it. It will make my regular workflow much more convenient! Wireshark is a fantastic suite of tools and I hope other people will also find this feature valuable.

Should I make a note in the documentation that compression is supported and also warn that loading large lz4/zstd compressed pcaps is not recommended?

> Wireshark already stores the dissection result in RAM

Where does it do that?

Note that, when ~~Wireshark~~Ethereal (yes, it was that long ago) was first made to, when dissecting, build a protocol tree rather than just building a GTK+ display tree, there was a bug that meant that the protocol trees were leaked.  I noticed this because my machine started thrashing when loading a large file; fixing the leak fixed the problem.

commits_data.title: Add support for ZSTD and LZ4 decompression
commits_data.message:
Add support for ZSTD and LZ4 decompression

- Describe zstd and lz4 support in man pages
- Update AUTHORS
- Update mime types to recognize zstd and lz4
